## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k for game 28, review the last game, and focus on securing enough area with room for reductions. I’ll save every returned position before continuing.

# Game 27: Black vs 20k — W+2

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Consecutive passes at moves 64–65 ended the game.
Official W+2 agrees with independent Black 43, White 38+7=45.
Final captures: Black 3, White 0. Every Black stone survived; no dead stones remained displayed.
The 20k record is four wins, eighteen losses and one draw. Retain 20k.

## Records and verification

- game-027.sgf contains all 65 moves: 62 stone moves and three passes.
- game-027-log.json saves opponent selection, all 33 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty and empty-region inventories, move notes, independent final area and historical replay checks.
- Historical replay of the actual moves reproduced all 33 returned play boards and capture counts. Capture events were B J7 at 53 (J8/J9) and B G8 at 55 (G9).
- No invalid move, attempted ko recapture, actual ko or resignation occurred.
- The initial log-format patch was refused before the first move; it was corrected before play. No response was lost.
- Code inspected boards, kept records, counted area, converted recorded moves to SGF and replayed actual historical moves. All choices and hypothetical reading were manual. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation.

## Opening: connected opposite bases, but no reduction margin

1 B C3, 2 W E5, 3 B G7, 4 W C6,
5 B E3, 6 W G3, 7 B E7, 8 W D7,
9 B G5, 10 W F4, 11 B E4, 12 W F5,
13 B G6, 14 W G4, 15 B C5, 16 W D4,
17 B D3, 18 W D5, 19 B C4, 20 W E6.

C3/G7 supplied opposite footholds. E3/E4 developed the lower central boundary; E7/G5 expanded the upper region before enclosure. G6 directly joined G5/G7. C5 started disconnected with B5/C4/D5. After White D4, D3 directly joined C3/E3 and prevented a lower cut. White D5 reduced C5 to B5/C4; C4 promptly connected it to the lower group.

The selected early outline after move 10 was exactly 45:
E/F/G/H/J rows 7–9 =15;
G/H/J rows 5–6 =6;
A–E rows 1–3 =15;
A–D row 4 =4;
A–C row 5 =3;
F1/F2 =2.
This was selected room with many unplayed boundaries, not secure ownership or a forecast.
It contained no reduction margin above Black's minimum winning 45.

White D4 occupied one selected point, while Black E4 supplied a different row-4 boundary point. The revised lower selection was:
A–E rows 1–3 =15, F1/F2 =2,
A–C row 4 plus E4 =4, A–C row 5 =3, total 24.
The upper selection was still 21. No group yet had a two-eye proof.

## Upper boundary reduction and prompt connections

21 B F7, 22 W E8, 23 B F8, 24 W E9,
25 B F9, 26 W C8, 27 B B5, 28 W H5,
29 B H6, 30 W J5, 31 B J6, 32 W H4.

F7 joined the two-liberty E7 stone to G7. F8 then preserved top access; F9 secured the first-line boundary after E9. White E8/E9 formed one group: a White F9 continuation would join E9, not be an isolated stone automatically captured by G9.

E8/E9 removed two points from the selected upper region. Its revised 19 was F/G/H/J rows 7–9 =12, E7 =1, G/H/J rows 5–6 =6. With lower 24, the conditional total was already 43.

B5 secured the lower-left boundary and prepared B6. White H5/J5 occupied two more upper target points. H6 and J6 capped this entry with direct connections; White H4 joined it to G4. Upper became 17:
G5 =1; G/H/J row 6 =3;
E/F/G/H/J row 7 =5; F/G/H/J rows 8–9 =8.
Lower 24 plus upper 17 was only 41.

The territorial deficit was identified during play. Repairs retained life and area, but could not alone restore a winning margin. Earlier E8 instead of F7 at 21 is only a candidate: it would leave F7 unconnected and needs a full boundary/cut assessment. No saving or winning replacement was verified.

## Lower expansion: real gains, then answered undercuts

33 B F2, 34 W G2, 35 B B6, 36 W B7,
37 B F3, 38 W F1, 39 B E1, 40 W G1,
41 B E2, 42 W A6, 43 B A5, 44 W A7,
45 B F6, 46 W C7.

F2 began disconnected with E2/F1/G2. White G2 removed one route but F2 retained E2/F1/F3. B6 directly joined B5 and expanded the selected lower region by B6/A6, from 24 to 26. F3 then actually joined F2 to E3 and added one boundary point, giving lower 27 plus upper 17 =44, a draw outline.

White F1 took one selected point. E1 blocked its left undercut, initially with D1/E2 as liberties. The considered White E2 cut would be isolated with only D2: D2 joins existing D3 and captures it. This was manual local reading, not an actual sequence. Actual White G1 joined F1 to G2; no forced capture of F1 existed. E2 then connected E1 through E3/F2.

White A6 removed another selected lower point. A5 safely joined B5 and ataried A6 at A7, but White A7 simply connected B7. The threat was safe and answered; it supplied no capture. Lower fell to 25.

F6 directly joined F7/G6 and gained the remaining central boundary point. It added no liberty, but the upper group retained G8/G9/H7/J7. Upper became 18, total 43.

The exact accounting was:
45 early target;
minus E8/E9 ->43;
minus H5/J5 ->41;
plus B6/A6 ->43;
plus F3 ->44;
minus F1 ->43;
minus A6 ->42;
plus F6 ->43.
These were revisions of one selected outline, not secure counts until life and boundaries were checked.

Earlier A6 instead of E2 at 41 is an unverified boundary candidate. E1 would still be disconnected and its actual cut/capture routes would need checking. Merely retaining A6, with every other final point unchanged, would give 44 and a draw, not a win. Two shifted points from the actual final split are needed to win. Earlier development must seek a margin, not just recover one point.

## Upper invasion defense: rebuild after each capture

47 B H7, 48 W J8, 49 B H8, 50 W J9,
51 B H9, 52 W G9,
53 B J7 captured J8/J9, 54 W pass,
55 B G8 captured G9, 56 W C9.

H7 directly joined G7/H6. H8 joined H7 and blocked J8's central route.
After White J9, the two White stones had exactly H9/J7.
H9 joined H8 and left them only J7; the upper Black group retained G8/G9/J7.
White J7 would add no liberty and capture nothing because Black retained G8/G9, so it was suicide.

White instead invaded G9, which had only G8. Black then had G8/J7; both White invader groups were in atari.
J7 captured the TWO J8/J9 stones. This reopened J8/J9 for Black: upper liberties were G8/J8/J9.
White G8 would join G9 but have no liberty; it could not capture Black because Black retained the reopened right space. It was suicide.

G8 captured G9. Final true eyes:
- G9, with F9/G8/H9 boundaries.
- J8/J9, with H8/H9/J7 boundaries.
All boundaries are one connected fifteen-stone Black group.
Fifteen stones plus three territory points =18.

The captures restored the existing outline; they did not expand it. Do not credit White's failed invasions as a forced opening gain. No ko occurred: J7 captured two stones, and G8's one-stone capture joined an already connected group with another eye.

## Lower life and final White life check

57 B C2, 58 W D9, 59 B D1, 60 W J3,
61 B B2, 62 W H2, 63 B B1,
64 W pass, 65 B pass.

C2 joined C3. D1 joined E1 and secured D2, bounded by C2/D1/D3/E2.
B2 joined C2; B1 joined B2 and secured C1, bounded by B1/C2/D1.
All boundaries were one connected seventeen-stone Black group. C1/D2 are independent true eyes.
Seventeen stones plus eight territory points =25. No Black stone was lost.

White upper group had true D8 and the separate A8/A9/B8/B9 corner room.
White's lower main group and isolated J3 shared true H3/J4:
H3 boundaries G3/H2/H4/J3;
J4 boundaries H4/J3/J5.
All are White. Both groups retain the other eye if Black tries either fill, so neither is captured and either Black fill is suicide. This is same-color shared-eye life, despite J3 remaining disconnected. Do not confuse it with opposing-color shared-liberty traps.

All displayed stones were alive; no manual dead-stone removal was needed.

## Independent final area

Black 32 stones +11 territory =43.
Lower 25, upper 18.
Black empty regions: A1/A2/A3/A4/B3/B4 (6), C1 (1), D2 (1), G9 (1), J8/J9 (2).
Rows 1–9 Black: 5,6,6,4,4,5,5,4,4.

White 27 stones +11 territory =38.
White empty regions: A8/A9/B8/B9 (4), D8 (1), D6 (1), H3 (1), J4 (1), H1/J1/J2 (3).
Rows 1–9 White: 4,3,3,5,5,4,4,5,5.
No neutral points. Black43 versus White38+7=45 gives W+2.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k: four wins, eighteen losses, one draw.
2. Preserve prompt actual connections G6, D3/C4, F7/F8/F9, H6/J6, F3/E2 and C2/D1/B2/B1. Every Black stone survived, with no rescue relying on an ignored atari.
3. A minimum 45-point conditional opening outline has no reduction margin. E8/E9 and H5/J5 removed four points before lower expansion; final F1/A6 undercuts offset most gains.
4. Expand needed endpoints before local repairs consume the available turns. Earlier E8 or A6 are hypotheses; a single extra point from this final split only draws.
5. Keep exact upper capture order and reopened-liberty proof: H9 atari, J7 captures two, G8 captures one. Three captures preserved eighteen area, not a winning expansion.
6. Check all boundary groups in shared eyes. White J3 and its main group were unconditionally alive through H3/J4 despite disconnection.
7. Count rows and actual stones/empty regions; outcomes and cleaner survival do not establish repeatable strength or individual move values.

# Game 10: White vs 20k — W+10

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 63–64. There were 64 moves: 61 stone moves and three passes (61, 63, 64).
Final captures: Black 0, White 4. No ko, invalid move, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

This is the first win in the series, following five losses at 20k. It establishes one successful game at 20k, not consistent strength or an optimal opening. Retain 20k until wins and living groups are repeatable, including as Black.

## Records and verified score
- game-010.sgf contains all 64 moves.
- game-010-log.json contains opponent selection, all 32 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty inventories, complete moves and independent area count.
- Official result: White wins by 10 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 26 stones + 13 territory = 39; White 31 stones + 11 territory = 42. White plus komi = 49. All 81 points are assigned; no neutral points.
- White's lower group: 14 stones plus E1/D2/D3 = 17 area.
- White's upper group: 17 stones plus A9/C8/D9/E9/F9/G9/H9/J9 = 25 area.
- Upper area by rows: all nine points in row 9, all nine in row 8, B7/C7/D7/E7/G7 (five), and C6/D6 (two): 25.
- Black territory: A5 and H1/J1/H2/J2/H3/J3/H4/J4/G5/H5/J5/J6.
- Black captured no White stones. The four captured Black stones were E1 at move 24 and C2/D2/D3 at move 26.

## Lower fight: cut, pressure the shared escape, then secure the eyes
Opening:
1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D3, 4 W C4, 5 B C5,
6 W D4, 7 B D5, 8 W E3, 9 B D2,
10 W E4, 11 B F4, 12 W F3, 13 B G4.

E3 put D3 in atari, and Black D2 extended downward. E4 joined E3 to C3/C4/D4; F3 extended into still-open lower-right space. Unlike the late E4 extension in game 8, this extension had more than one temporary destination.

14 W C7 established an upper foothold while the lower group still had options.
15 B B4, 16 W B3, 17 B C2, 18 W B2,
19 B B1, 20 W E2, 21 B E1.

B3/B2 answered the left-side pressure, but B1 undercut the first-line boundary. The group was not yet alive. After move 21, Black C2/D2/D3 had only C1/D1; Black E1 had D1/F1.

22 W F1 reduced E1 to D1. Black ignored this atari with 23 B A4.
24 W D1 captured E1 and put C2/D2/D3 in atari at C1.
Black ignored that atari with 25 B A3.
26 W C1 captured C2/D2/D3.
27 B A2 kept Black B1 in atari at A1 while connecting the left-edge Black stones.

F1 before D1 mattered. In the actual move-21 position, immediate W D1 would be a self-atari at C1; B C1 captures that stone and opens D1 for the Black group. After F1, W D1 instead captures E1, opening E1 as a second liberty for the new White stone.

Black's ignored ataris were concrete mistakes. The opening is not proven to force the played captures. A short manual alternative after W F1 is B D1 connecting E1 to C2/D2/D3; that joined five-stone Black group would have only C1, where White can capture it. This limited reading is not a proof of every alternative or a forced win.

The capture at C1 did not itself prove life. White C1/D1 and F1 were still separate from the main group, and the empty C2/D2/D3 region was connected.
28 W F2 connected F1 to E2/F3.
29 B B5, 30 W C2 connected C1/D1 through B2/C3 and closed the left boundary of D2/D3.

After move 30 the lower group had two independent secured eye spaces:
- E1: bounded by White D1/E2/F1, all connected.
- D2/D3: bounded by White D1/C2/E2/C3/E3/D4, all connected.
This life proof held when Black G3/G2/G1 closed the remaining outside liberties. The final lower group had exactly E1/D2/D3 as liberties and was alive.

White did not chase the atari Black B1 by W A1 after move 27. That would capture B1 but leave the new isolated A1 stone with only B1, introducing a simple-ko dependency. F2/C2 secured unconditional eyes elsewhere instead.

## Upper development: make the second base large enough and repair each connection
31 B G3, 32 W E7, 33 B G2, 34 W G7, 35 B G1.
The lower group stayed alive but shrank to 17 area. The earlier C7 foothold allowed White to develop the open upper side, rather than attempting another late lower-right invasion.

36 W C6, 37 B F5, 38 W D6, 39 B B6,
40 W B7, 41 B A7, 42 W A8, 43 B A6,
44 W B8, 45 B E6, 46 W D7.

B8 immediately joined A8 to B7. A8 had only B8/A9 after Black A6; leaving it disconnected would have allowed further pressure. D7 then joined the left upper chain to E7.

47 B F7 cut between E7 and G7, with only F6/F8.
48 W F8 put it in atari; 49 B F6 connected it to Black's main group.
50 W E8 connected F8 to the left upper chain.
51 B G6 left White G7 only H7/G8.
52 W G8 joined G7 to F8 before 53 B H7 removed H7.
54 W H8, 55 B H6, 56 W J8 closed the upper-right boundary.
57 B A1 connected Black B1 to the main group.
58 W D8, 59 B J7.

The choice of F8 rather than F6 at move 48 avoided a counter-atari trap: W F6 would have only G6, and B G6 could capture it, reopening F6 for Black F7. The actual F8 had E8/G8/F9 and supplied a viable connection.

## Settle the eyes before accepting the winning count
60 W B9, 61 B pass, 62 W C9, 63 B pass, 64 W pass.

B9 first connected to B8 and made a true eye at A9, bounded by A8/B9.
C9 then connected through B9 and made a second true eye at C8, bounded by B8/C7/D8/C9.
All boundaries belong to the connected upper group. D9–J9 remained a third, larger eye space.

C9 would not have connected directly to B8 or D8: those are diagonal neighbors. The actual B9–C9 sequence supplied the stone connection needed for the life proof.

The formal row/region count came late, around moves 52–63: 17 lower plus 25 upper = 42, enough to beat Black's 39 with komi. Early area estimates were provisional and were not recorded as a detailed secure/potential count around moves 10–16. Improve that timing next game; this win does not erase the counting weakness.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k for repeatability, especially as Black. One win does not establish consistent strength.
2. A small living group can anchor a winning total if a second base is developed while open space remains. Here 17 lower + 25 upper won; no late right-side invasion was needed.
3. Use the capture's newly opened liberty explicitly. F1 before D1 meant D1 captured E1 and survived; immediate D1 would have been captured.
4. Finish connections and eye boundaries after a capture. F2/C2 established E1 and D2/D3; the capture alone did not.
5. Repair short-liberty stones before tenuki: A8–B8, F8–E8, and G7–G8 all survived. Check the new atari stone too: F6 would have failed to G6.
6. Name actual orthogonal connections, not diagonals. B9 before C9 produced two independent true eyes A9/C8.
7. Count by rows earlier. Preserve the separation between secure area and unsecured outlines even when the opponent plays weakly.

Code only parsed returned current boards, counted present groups/liberties and empty regions, recorded responses, and converted the move record to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

Goal: improve at 9x9 Go across fresh sessions, ultimately win consistently against human-style KataGo 9d.

- Game 2: White vs 4k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 49 (J6). No captures or numerical final score.
- Game 3: Black vs 8k, same rules. Lost by resignation after White move 64 (J5). Final captures: Black 1, White 2; no numerical final score.
- Game 4: White vs 12k, same rules. Lost by resignation after Black move 43 (F1). Final captures: Black 1, White 0; no numerical final score.

Final captures: Black 4, White 16; White captured fifteen left-side stones after winning the A1 ko for life. The right group lived with three independent two-point eye spaces.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.

White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.
23. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. In game 7, F9 had only F8/G9 and was disconnected from E8. Black G2 allowed White F8/G8 to trap the top stones. F8 before tenuki is an unverified candidate connecting F9 to E8, not an established winning move.
24. A counter-atari may release the opponent when they capture first. After game 7's Black F7 at move 47, White F8/G8 had only H8, but Black F9/G9 had only H9. White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.
25. A diagonal framework also needs a concrete area count. Game 7's vague estimate of about 45 was unsupported; the later row count gave only 38 potential points even with the top intact. Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.
26. Empty prospective eye points need secured boundaries and enough turns. Game 7's G2 invasion lost its right route to White H2 and its left route to White F2. Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.
27. Three corner approaches are not three living bases. In game 8, White C7/C3/G7/E7 built a surviving top wall, but C3 was left alone until move 22. After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.
28. An extension into one temporary liberty is not an escape. In game 8, White E4 added F4, which Black immediately occupied. The corner could not save the group: after move 35, W B2, B A2, W B1, B A1 captures ten. Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
29. An edge strip also needs an outside boundary. Game 8's H3/H2/H1 had only J3/J2/J1 after Black H4/G2/G1. J4 was unsecured, so these were not two eyes. Black J3/J2/J1 captured all three; White J1 was suicide because Black J2/J3 retained J4. Do not reuse this late entry as a living pattern.
